performers: Mary Garden, soprano; Claude Debussy, piano
question: What changes when the accompaniment falls away and a character sings almost to herself?
intro: Mary Garden, the first Mélisande, records the tower song with Debussy at the piano in 1904. The scene places Mélisande at a window combing her loosened hair. Much of the song is written for the voice alone, with instrumental phrases around it; the sparse setting makes the singer’s line unusually exposed.

cues.title: A voice with space around it
cues.text: The score frames Mélisande’s song with instrumental phrases, leaving much of her vocal line unaccompanied. Listen for the difference between a piano passage and a sung phrase without harmonic support underneath. The pauses between them belong to the scene’s intimacy.
cues.evidence: Fromont1902 vocal score, printed pp.102–104 (PDF108–110): https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/d/d6/IMSLP33280-PMLP09094-Debussy-L088vsFR.pdf. The report records a quiet opening and a change around0:28; no exact voice entrance is asserted.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The first Mélisande sings again
cues.text: Garden is the Mélisande named in the original 1902 score’s cast list. Two years later she records this excerpt with its composer. The connection is unusually direct, although a short acoustic disc cannot reproduce the whole theatrical performance.
cues.evidence: Fromont1902 vocal score, cast list(PDF5), names Garden as Mélisande. BnF subnotice7 records Garden, Debussy and1904: https://catalogue.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/cb38388874b. This is historical context, not a claim of identical stage and recorded delivery.

cues.title: Words shape an unaccompanied line
cues.text: The later lines invoke saints and remember a Sunday birth. In the score, the voice again sings without a continuous accompaniment. Listen to how a short phrase can keep its direction through held notes and gaps when a pianist is not marking every beat.
cues.evidence: Fromont score pp.103–104: Saint Daniel/Saint Michel/Saint Raphaël and the Sunday-birth lines, with rests in the accompaniment. Strong report changes at1:06 and1:18 locate the later region only; individual words are not aligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A transfer speed is documented

cues.evidence: Internet Archive metadata description: https://archive.org/metadata/78_meslongscheveux_010_14/metadata. No tuning value or corrected historical tempo is inferred from the speed setting.

transitions.title: The voice resumes after the instrumental link
transitions.how: The first part of the song gives way to an instrumental link before the voice continues with its invocation. Debussy does not turn that continuation into a fully accompanied aria: the exposed vocal line remains central, and the piano returns around it rather than filling every gap. The change is small in forces but clear in the alternation of speech-like singing and instrumental space.
transitions.evidence: Fromont vocal score pp.103–104, after the repeated “Et tout le long du jour” and before the saints’ names; accompaniment rests during most vocal phrases. Report: quieter1:00 window followed by strong1:06 change. The66s marker is an approximate passage boundary.

timeline.note: The piano introduces the scene with repeated figures and held tones.
Mélisande’s first stanza is largely unaccompanied in the score.
A short instrumental link overlaps the first stanza’s final held note, then continues alone.
The invocation and the Sunday-birth lines again leave the voice exposed.
The piano carries the closing instrumental phrase.

composer.background:
Debussy was born above his parents’ china shop in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, outside Paris. Neither parent was a professional musician. His father’s involvement in the Paris Commune brought imprisonment in 1871; through a connection made during that imprisonment, the boy came to the piano teacher Antoinette Mauté, Verlaine’s mother-in-law. He entered the Paris Conservatoire in 1872, aged ten. Antoine Marmontel trained him as a pianist; Ernest Guiraud later taught him composition. His resistance to harmonic rules developed inside this education: he could play, analyse and compete successfully in the system he came to distrust.

From 1880 he spent summers working for Nadezhda von Meck, Tchaikovsky’s patron, playing chamber music and teaching her children. Travel with her household took him to Italy and Russia. In Paris he accompanied the soprano Marie Vasnier, with whom he had an affair, and wrote songs for her flexible high voice. In their accompaniments, the piano’s register, resonance and passing harmonic changes can supply a second interpretation of the words. The early songs also show how thoroughly he knew the French vocal tradition he would alter.
